title: Ms. Ludgate-Dwyer Goes To Washington

jokes.text: Well, it is simple, Leslie. In today's fast-paced society, National Parks are still the best place for full-moon werewolf transformations.
jokes.setup: Leslie is earnestly drilling April on why senators should invest in the National Park Service, expecting a prepared, policy-ready answer.
jokes.punchline: April deadpans the most absurd, anti-professional answer possible: werewolf transformations.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly in character for April — her deadpan delivery of absurd, gothic nonsense is her comedic signature. The structure is tight: Leslie sets up a straight policy question, April detonates it with maximum specificity (full-moon werewolf transformations). The phrase 'in today's fast-paced society' mimics the cadence of a real answer, which makes the punchline hit harder. Strong character integration — no other Parks character could deliver this line.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: National Parks are a crucial habitat for werewolves. Without them, werewolves would be forced into urban areas where they'd have to eat people. So really, you're saving lives.

jokes.text: I know you're kidding, but I also know that you're prepared, and we are going to do great.
jokes.setup: April just gave a completely absurd answer about werewolf transformations.
jokes.punchline: Leslie, ever the relentless optimist, chooses to interpret the chaos as evidence of preparedness, refusing to acknowledge the absurdity.
jokes.explanation: The joke is Leslie's oblivious, hyper-positive spin on April's trolling. It's a reliable comedic beat for her character — the audience laughs at the gap between April's nihilism and Leslie's relentless positivity. Good character integration, though it's a familiar Leslie move rather than a fresh one.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We're a great team! We work together so well, we communicate, we support each other...

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We're also all going to die alone.

jokes.text: Yeah. Also, you have lipstick on your teeth.
jokes.setup: Leslie is being warmly enthusiastic about their partnership, building emotional momentum with 'We're a great team.'
jokes.punchline: April deflates it instantly with a mundane, slightly humiliating non-sequitur about lipstick.
jokes.explanation: Brutally economical. Leslie's warm sentiment is punctured by April's casually deflating observation — not cruel, just withholding emotional reciprocity. The 'Yeah. Also...' construction is a masterclass in comedic timing on the page. It's quintessential April: she can't quite let sincerity land without undermining it.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I know what's going on in your head right now.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: My mind is a Terrordome. A vast, barren wasteland where a few scattered remnants of human thought fight to the death for survival.

jokes.text: Oh! Well, then, welcome to the Terrordome.
jokes.setup: Leslie says warmly that she thinks she knows what's going on in April's head.
jokes.punchline: April responds with a hip-hop cultural reference (Public Enemy's 'Welcome to the Terrordome') to describe the interior of her mind, which is both absurd and perfectly characterful.
jokes.explanation: Funny because of the gap between the sweet Leslie-April moment and the aggressive imagery of a Public Enemy track. Also self-aware: April is acknowledging her own chaotic inner world. The reference has just enough specificity to reward viewers who catch it without being exclusionary.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Leslie freaks out whenever anything changes. Like, anything at all.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I got a trim! A TRIM, April! My entire life is falling apart!

jokes.text: What? Why? On what grounds? Those fonts are perfect. It's readable and compact. It's all on one page. That's insane. Don't mess with that. I appreciate your initiative, but itineraries are not the right place to mess around.
jokes.setup: April, testing whether Leslie can handle change, asks about changing the font on the itineraries.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's escalating, increasingly intense defense of the itinerary fonts — treating font choice as a serious professional matter — confirms April's fears that Leslie cannot handle any change.
jokes.explanation: 'On what grounds?' and 'itineraries are not the right place to mess around' are the standout lines. The escalation of Leslie's legal/official language applied to font selection is pitch-perfect Leslie obsessiveness. The fact that this was April's 'test' makes it funnier in retrospect.

jokes.text: One time, Andy told her that I was getting rid of my bangs and she called 911.
jokes.setup: Ben (in a talking-head confessional) is trying to convince April to tell Leslie she wants to leave her job, saying Leslie can be open-minded.
jokes.punchline: April's counter-example is that Leslie called 911 over a minor cosmetic change — the absurd escalation perfectly illustrates Leslie's catastrophizing.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Extremely specific, extremely Leslie, and the escalation (bangs → 911) is perfectly calibrated. The joke is both a character illustration of Leslie AND a character illustration of April's weary relationship with her. It's quotable, instantly memorable, and earns its laughs entirely through character logic. Rewatch bonus: on rewatch, you appreciate how well it foreshadows Leslie's later meltdown about April quitting.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: What if we just changed the font?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Changed the font? CHANGED THE FONT?! April, fonts are the very foundation of visual communication! You can't just change a font like you're redecorating a sorority house! A font is a sacred trust between a designer and their audience. It's typography, April. It's ART. Do you know how many hours I spent selecting our current font? Seventy-two. Seventy-two hours. And now you want to just... change it? Like it's nothing? Like it's some kind of... of casual decision? This is exactly the kind of reckless thinking that leads to the downfall of civilizations, April. The Romans fell because they stopped caring about their fonts. Look it up.

jokes.text: Any time your name comes up, I panic and change the subject to the Twin Peaks reboot until she gets bored. So, you talk for one second?
jokes.setup: Ben is trying to convince April to tell Leslie she wants to leave, but he admits he can't keep the secret.
jokes.punchline: His coping mechanism — pivoting to the Twin Peaks reboot — is both very specific and very funny. The follow-up 'So, you talk for one second?' is April's deadpan callback that Twin Peaks is famously convoluted/polarizing.
jokes.explanation: Two-layered joke: the specificity of 'Twin Peaks reboot' is funny on its own (it's such a nerdy/specific choice for Ben), and April's 'you talk for one second' implies the reboot is so confusing/dense that Leslie tunes out immediately. The exchange has great rhythm.

jokes.text: She'll drown me in the Potomac while she recites facts about the Potomac.
jokes.setup: April is explaining why she won't tell Leslie she's leaving on this trip.
jokes.punchline: The image of Leslie drowning April while delivering Potomac trivia is both darkly violent and a perfect distillation of Leslie's obsessive enthusiasm clashing with April's fate.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. It's simultaneously character comedy for Leslie (the facts detail captures her perfectly) AND character comedy for April (the dark, macabre framing). The specificity of 'while she recites facts about the Potomac' elevates a basic murder joke into something genuinely inspired. Highly quotable, tight, and could only work for these two characters. Approaches the top anchor standard.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, I got April's job requirements list right here.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Let's see... 'Dreamboat,' 'Cool Guy,' 'The Velociraptor'...

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh no, this is my desired nicknames list.

jokes.text: Apple juice, barbecue sauce, Count Chocula... Wait. Oh, sorry. That's the list of cool new nicknames I want people to call me.
jokes.setup: Andy is helping April figure out what she wants in a new job; he says they have a list.
jokes.punchline: The 'list' turns out to be a list of food-based nicknames Andy wants for himself — a complete non-sequitur that reveals Andy's gleeful self-absorption and childlike priorities.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Andy joke. The list of food items as desired nicknames (Apple juice, barbecue sauce, Count Chocula) is delightfully specific and weird, and his breezy 'Wait. Oh, sorry.' treats it as a completely reasonable mistake. The joke works because it's so perfectly Andy — enthusiastic, well-meaning, and entirely off-task. Count Chocula as a desired nickname is a particular gem.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: From now on, call me Beastmaster. Beastmaster Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, no. Just Andy. Regular Andy.

jokes.text: Yeah. Ben Wyatt, please? Tell him it's Count Chocula.
jokes.setup: Andy is calling Ben to help April find a job; he announces his decision to use the nickname he just invented.
jokes.punchline: He immediately puts 'Count Chocula' into practice by using it as his phone alias, the callback landing instantly after the nickname list joke.
jokes.explanation: The quick callback deepens the previous joke — Andy isn't just fantasizing about nicknames, he's already deploying them. The self-assurance of immediately using Count Chocula as an official alias is very Andy. Good economy and timing.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You're a secret agent, aren't you? No wait, you're a CIA operative. Actually, you're definitely a black ops assassin for the government.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I work in construction.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That's... not what I was going for.

jokes.text: No, it's Andrew Dwyer. I'm sorry.
jokes.setup: Andy has just asked the receptionist to tell Ben Wyatt that 'Count Chocula' is calling.
jokes.punchline: Andy immediately backs down and gives his real name, revealing that either the receptionist pushed back or (funnier) Andy lost his nerve about the nickname in real-time.
jokes.explanation: The deflation of the Count Chocula bit is itself the punchline — Andy's confidence evaporating when faced with an actual person is endearing and funny. The apology adds to it. A nice topper on the callback chain.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Welcome. This is the front entrance. As you can see, it has a door. The door opens and closes. Very reliable.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Over here we have a window. Natural light comes through it during the day. At night, it becomes a mirror.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: This is a wall. It's load-bearing. If we removed it, everything above it would fall down. I've tested this theory. It's sound.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: And this is my office. Notice the desk. It's made of wood. Wood comes from trees. The government used to own the trees. Now I do.

jokes.text: I always knew she would tire of government. Took long enough.
jokes.setup: Andy tells Ron that April wants to leave government and they're trying to help her find a new job.
jokes.punchline: Ron's response is characteristically approving of anyone leaving government — his anti-government libertarianism expressed as mild impatience that it took April this long.
jokes.explanation: Classic Ron joke — his worldview expressed as mild, dismissive approval. 'Took long enough' is the key phrase, suggesting he's been waiting years for this. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, is Don your brother?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Yes.

jokes.text: I'm guessing it's a business? Assassins? Hit men? [Ron] Doctors. [Andy] You guys are doctors? [Ron] We build things.
jokes.setup: Andy admits he doesn't know what Ron's company does, and starts guessing.
jokes.punchline: The escalation from 'business' to 'assassins' to 'hit men' followed by Ron's deadpan 'Doctors' (also wrong, apparently) and the correction 'We build things' is a layered exchange that plays Andy's obliviousness against Ron's terse pragmatism.
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: Andy's absurd guesses and the fact that Ron momentarily says 'doctors' before correcting it, suggesting even he stumbles around the explanation. The quick escalation to 'assassins/hit men' is vintage Andy logic.

dialogue.speaker: Don
dialogue.line: You know, Ron, you've got quite a history with the Parks Department.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's enough. Tour's over. Everyone out.

jokes.text: This is a door. These, of course, are walls. What else? What else? Ah.
jokes.setup: Ron offers to show Andy and Ben around his company.
jokes.punchline: The 'tour' consists of Ron pointing out basic architectural features as if they were noteworthy, delivered with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Ron's terse pragmatism expressed as an intentionally useless tour. 'These, of course, are walls' is the standout line — the 'of course' elevates it from deadpan to arch. The 'What else? What else?' pause suggests he genuinely can't think of anything more interesting to show them. Very economical, very Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I was just having fun about making matching shirts.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No, you didn't.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, I made them.

jokes.text: Meet our vice president, Don Swanson. [Andy] Is this your brother? You have a brother? [Ron] No. Fine. Yes, suppose the cat's out of the bag. I have a brother. One brother.
jokes.setup: Ron introduces his VP, Don Swanson, to Andy and Ben.
jokes.punchline: Andy immediately clocks the resemblance and exposes that Ron has been hiding a brother — Ron's deeply private nature extended to concealing even the existence of a sibling from longtime colleagues.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed character joke: the VP having Ron's last name should have been a tell, but Ron's extreme privacy meant he never mentioned a brother. 'Fine. Yes, suppose the cat's out of the bag' is a perfectly Ron-ish surrender, and 'One brother' is precise in a way that implies there might be more surprises. The rewatch bonus is that on rewatch, you wonder what else Ron has hidden in plain sight.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What kind of building are they constructing?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: A parking garage. It's going to have spaces for cars, and also some spaces for cars.

jokes.text: Ron: 'Tour is over.' — abruptly ending the factory tour the moment his brother secret is out.
jokes.setup: Ben and Andy are marveling that Ron never mentioned a brother after years at Parks.
jokes.punchline: Ron immediately shuts everything down — 'Tour is over' — rather than engage with any emotional revelation.
jokes.explanation: Three words, maximum Ron. The economy is exceptional — he doesn't explain, doesn't apologize, just terminates. Deeply character-specific and gets funnier because it's so blunt.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Ron, don't you think there are a lot of creative problem solving opportunities in government?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: No. And I don't want there to be. Creativity is a Latin word, meaning 'to make something.' If I have to make something, it means I don't have enough. Government should not encourage creativity. We should discourage it.

jokes.text: All those years together at the Parks Department, and you never told us you had a brother. [Ron] You worked at the Parks Department? [Ron] Tour is over.
jokes.setup: Andy and Ben are reacting with surprise to Ron's hidden brother.
jokes.punchline: Ben's revelation that he worked at the Parks Department causes Ron to immediately shut down the entire tour — suggesting that working in government is a greater revelation (and offense) than the secret brother.
jokes.explanation: 'Tour is over' — two words that land as a perfect punchline. Ron's anti-government sentiment is so deep that discovering Ben is a government man outweighs the secret brother drama. The beat where Ron seemingly didn't know Ben worked at Parks is also funny — these are supposedly friends. Economy is excellent. Escalation from brother reveal to tour cancellation is sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Don
dialogue.line: There's apparently an established method for stacking vinyl sheets.

jokes.text: Okay. Carry-on bags packed, trashy magazines purchased, boarding passes in hand, and we have 26 minutes for unstructured chat time.
jokes.setup: Leslie and April are at the airport before their flight to D.C.
jokes.punchline: Leslie has scheduled '26 minutes for unstructured chat time' — the comic irony being that scheduling spontaneous conversation renders it completely structured.
jokes.explanation: Classic Leslie joke — the oxymoron of scheduled 'unstructured' time is perfectly her. 'Trashy magazines purchased' is a nice character detail suggesting Leslie allows herself small, planned indulgences. The precision of '26 minutes' is better than a round number.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'd just tell him that Grimace is a blob of undefined physicality.

jokes.text: Ta-da! This is your clear, definitive path through the federal government. It starts here today with this flight and it goes all the way to 2022.
jokes.setup: Leslie tells April she wants to talk about her future during their chat time, and April nervously thinks Leslie might be onto her plan to quit.
jokes.punchline: Leslie produces a binder/chart mapping out April's entire federal government career through 2022 — total planning mania dressed up as a gift.
jokes.explanation: The visual gag of Leslie producing an elaborate career binder is very her — and the rewatch bonus is significant because this plan is about to be completely demolished. The 'Ta-da!' makes it extra funny — Leslie presenting April's life plan like a magic trick.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: April, I'm so excited to show you the historical significance of these lampposts. Did you know that President Theodore Roosevelt walked past this very spot in 1902?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Actually, I met with President Roosevelt last week. We discussed economic policy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: April, that's impossible. Theodore Roosevelt died in 1919.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I know. It was awkward.

jokes.text: I had to make some guesses about your ultimate government objectives and your fashion choices, etcetera.
jokes.setup: Leslie is explaining her career plan binder for April.
jokes.punchline: The inclusion of 'fashion choices' alongside 'government objectives' as things Leslie had to plan for April reveals the totality of Leslie's controlling enthusiasm — she's planned April's wardrobe for the next seven years.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'fashion choices' elevates what could be a generic Leslie-is-controlling joke into something funnier and more specific. The casual 'etcetera' implies there's more she's planned that she's not even mentioning.

jokes.text: What's up with these shirts? [Leslie] Just a little fun I was having, you know? I didn't really make the shirts. [April] But did you, though? [Leslie] Yes, I did.
jokes.setup: April notices something in the binder.
jokes.punchline: The reveal that Leslie made custom 'Leslie and April Washington D.C.' shirts (implied by context) and her attempt to play it cool before admitting she made them is a perfect Leslie beat.
jokes.explanation: The three-beat structure is excellent: 'But did you, though?' / 'Yes, I did.' Leslie's brief attempt to seem casual ('just a little fun') collapsing under April's simple follow-up is very well timed. Short, sharp, effective.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Hey guys, it's great to see you all! I've actuarily missed working with you.

jokes.text: But did you, though? / Yes, I did. / Ta-da!
jokes.setup: Leslie insists she didn't make matching shirts. April presses her.
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately caves and confirms she did, using her signature 'Ta-da!' for the second time this episode — revealing the shirts are real and Leslie is incapable of hiding this.
jokes.explanation: The callback to 'Ta-da!' is a nice structural choice — Leslie's pride in her productions always gets the same unveiling energy. The rapid capitulation (she holds out for one line) is also funny.

dialogue.speaker: Senator
dialogue.line: Has anyone ever told you that your tenacity is intimidating?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes. Every day. Since I was seven years old.

jokes.text: Ta-da! Oh, and also, I have a middle seat. [Leslie] April!
jokes.setup: Leslie is processing the shirt reveal with good humor. April says 'Ta-da!' mimicking Leslie.
jokes.punchline: The callback 'Ta-da!' is followed immediately by the completely deflating announcement that April has a middle seat, turning the triumphant flourish into an anti-climax.
jokes.explanation: The callback of Leslie's 'Ta-da' followed by the most mundane anti-climax possible (a middle seat) is a neat structural joke. Leslie's horrified 'April!' treats this as seriously offensive, which adds a layer.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We're called 'The Decemberists' because we're trying to overthrow the government. Get it? Decemberists? December? December 1917? The Russian Revolution? We're very political.

jokes.text: So, what kind of building is it? [Ron] It's a large-scale storage unit for surplus vinyl sheeting.
jokes.setup: They're checking April's job requirements against a warehouse project Ron could offer her — she wants 'passionate interest in subject matter.'
jokes.punchline: The job Ron describes — storing surplus vinyl sheeting — is so aggressively boring that it functions as its own punchline.
jokes.explanation: Ron's deadpan delivery of comically joyless job descriptions is a reliable source of comedy here. 'Surplus vinyl sheeting' is specificity in service of boredom — it's not just boring, it's the exact kind of industrial tedium Ron would find noble.

dialogue.speaker: Barney
dialogue.line: What's April's college major?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: She studied the completely impractical 'Halloween Studies'

jokes.text: Creativity is for people with glasses who like to lie.
jokes.setup: Andy asks if April would have opportunities for 'creative problem solving' at the vinyl sheeting warehouse.
jokes.punchline: Ron dismisses creativity entirely with a magnificently specific, utterly sincere condemnation.
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and among the best Ron Swanson lines in the series. It approaches the top calibration anchor. The joke is perfectly structured: Andy asks an earnest question, Ron delivers a brief, definitive pronouncement that encapsulates his entire worldview in eight words. 'People with glasses who like to lie' is bizarre, specific, deeply wrong, and completely Ron — it sounds like something a gruff 19th-century craftsman would believe. The specificity of 'glasses' is what elevates it from a generic anti-creativity line to something genuinely original. Highly quotable, rewatch-rewarding, and could only come from this character.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Hey Barney, you know what they say about compound interest? It really... compounds the problem! Get it? Because it's compound, and it compounds? I'm gonna be honest, I have no idea what compound interest is, but I'm pretty sure that was hilarious.

jokes.text: Although I suppose she could use 'creative' ways to organize and stack the vinyl sheeting. [Andy] No, that's insane. [Ron] We use the Towson Method. It's tried and true.
jokes.setup: After dismissing creativity, Ron briefly considers whether April could apply it to the warehouse.
jokes.punchline: Andy immediately rejects this as insane, and Ron defends 'the Towson Method' — a made-up specific methodology for stacking vinyl sheeting — with complete seriousness.
jokes.explanation: The Towson Method is a wonderful invented detail — Ron's world has a specific, named, inviolable methodology for stacking vinyl sheeting. It's the kind of absurdist specificity that rewards the writers' commitment to the bit. Andy calling creative stacking 'insane' is also a funny reversal.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, so I have to have a confirmation hearing? That's like... that's like winning the lottery! Except instead of money, I get to sit in front of a bunch of people and answer questions about my qualifications.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: It's not really like winning the lottery.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, you're right. It's better. Because the odds of winning the lottery are like one in a million. But the odds of me getting confirmed? I'd say they're more like one in a thousand.

jokes.text: Ooh! Yeah. Let's grab some lunch and some ice cream and then maybe some after-ice-cream tacos. We'll just brainstorm. Maybe grab some snacks.
jokes.setup: Ron says he'll help find April a job but needs some food first.
jokes.punchline: Andy's enthusiastic planning of lunch escalates from reasonable (lunch) to dessert (ice cream) to a bizarre third course (after-ice-cream tacos) to just more snacks, revealing his childlike relationship with food.
jokes.explanation: 'After-ice-cream tacos' is the key phrase — the casual invention of a new meal category between dessert and snacks is pure Andy. The escalation from rational to irrational is smooth and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You're a wuss for not handling pressure.

dialogue.speaker: Retiree
dialogue.line: My wife just died.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh... I... I didn't know that.

jokes.text: April, when Randy brings up the river project, that is your cue to... Distract the guard so the Hamburglar can make his escape.
jokes.setup: Leslie is briefing April on their Senate meeting strategy, giving her a specific cue for when to interject.
jokes.punchline: April completes Leslie's sentence with a nonsensical heist scenario involving the Hamburglar — underscoring both her irreverence and her desire to derail Leslie's careful planning.
jokes.explanation: The Hamburglar is a very specific, very funny choice — an obscure fast food mascot pressed into a heist scenario. April's instinct to derail professional briefings with absurd non-sequiturs is perfect character comedy. The sentence-completion structure (Leslie sets up, April subverts) works well.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Her résumé was just a signed photo of ALF

jokes.text: Is she going to be okay? [Leslie] Yeah. It's just April. Trust me.
jokes.setup: An observer is concerned after April's Hamburglar comment.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's 'It's just April. Trust me.' is a weary but affectionate normalizing of April's behavior — the comedy is in how thoroughly Leslie has lowered the bar for April and considers this acceptable.
jokes.explanation: A functional relationship joke — Leslie's unquestioning endorsement of April's unhinged behavior is sweet and funny. 'It's just April' is a phrase that does a lot of work quickly.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I need someone to do some mindless work for me.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Jerry!

jokes.text: Well, I have another great idea. How about you and me, April, Randy, 'Historical Lampposts of D.C.' walking tour? Starts in 15 minutes. [April] Sounds great, but I do have an appointment with the President.
jokes.setup: After a successful Senate meeting, Leslie enthusiastically proposes a walking tour of historical lampposts.
jokes.punchline: April casually claims to have a meeting with the President as an excuse to escape — the absurdity of the claim delivered with complete deadpan.
jokes.explanation: Two-part joke: Leslie's proposal of a 'Historical Lampposts' tour is itself funny (vintage Leslie hyper-enthusiasm for the mundane), and April's presidential escape excuse is a good deadpan exit. The lamppost tour detail is the stronger element.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What do you see when you look at Washington?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: A hundred thousand people who are worse than me.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I see the heart of our democracy. A place where great men and women come to make a difference.

jokes.text: Can we come?
jokes.setup: April has said she has a meeting with the President.
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately and earnestly asks if they can come to the President meeting, treating April's obvious excuse as potentially real.
jokes.explanation: Three words that land perfectly. Leslie's immediate enthusiasm — and the camera-to-face cut it presumably prompts — is a masterpiece of economy. Her sincerity makes it funnier than if she were being sarcastic.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The pinnacle is having a bench.

jokes.text: What kind of a business is this? Is it, like, hit man or astronauts? [Barney] It's an accounting firm.
jokes.setup: Andy and Ben are visiting Barney's company to pitch April for a consulting job.
jokes.punchline: Andy's guess of 'hit man or astronauts' echoes his earlier guesses for Ron's company — suggesting these are his two mental categories for businesses.
jokes.explanation: A running gag callback — Andy has the same two guesses (hitman variants, improbable professions) for every business. The callback makes it funnier than the original because it reveals a pattern in Andy's limited worldview. 'Astronauts' is a funnier choice than 'doctors.'

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I've created a comprehensive five-year plan for your life. Career trajectory, romantic milestones, financial goals—

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You didn't even let me finish—

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No to all of it. The plan, the milestones, the goals. No.

jokes.text: Hey. It is 'actuarily' very good to see you guys.
jokes.setup: Ben is delighted to be recognized and welcomed at an accounting/actuarial firm.
jokes.punchline: Ben makes a nerdy accounting/actuarial pun — 'actuarily' instead of 'actually' — which is both a terrible and perfectly Ben pun.
jokes.explanation: Ben's financial nerd persona expressed as an accounting pun is on-brand. It's a groan-worthy pun done with enough self-awareness that it works — Ben is clearly delighted by it, which is itself funny. The extra beat 'They like me here' makes it land harder.

dialogue.speaker: Madeleine Albright
dialogue.line: I have negotiated with world leaders and survived the Cold War, but I have never seen anyone so excited about a half birthday.

jokes.text: Ben! [colleague] They like me here.
jokes.setup: Ben and his accounting pun have been received with enthusiasm by the staff.
jokes.punchline: Ben's delighted aside to Andy — 'They like me here' — reveals his deep need for validation from fellow numbers people, contrasted with how Andy definitely doesn't share this enthusiasm.
jokes.explanation: Three words, maximum character. Ben's joy at belonging somewhere is sweet and funny — the implication being he doesn't always feel this accepted. Short and effective.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I'm not too focused and driven.

dialogue.speaker: Madeleine Albright
dialogue.line: You just ate my salad while talking to me about your five-year plan.

jokes.text: I took the liberty of writing the inscription. All you have to do is sign. 'To Leslie, my inspiration, my muse, my partner in crime. I owe it all to you.' And there's room for a P.S. if you feel there's more you left out.
jokes.setup: Senator Gillibrand offers to sign a copy of her book for Leslie.
jokes.punchline: April has already written an extravagant self-aggrandizing inscription for Leslie and is asking the Senator to simply sign it — and then offers room for more.
jokes.explanation: Excellent character moment — April, who loves April, uses a Senator as a vehicle for Leslie-flattery. The inscription is over-the-top ('my inspiration, my muse, my partner in crime') and the offer of a P.S. is the topper. It's funny because April would normally never do something this earnestly nice for Leslie, but she's doing it through this bizarrely aggressive proxy. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Madeleine Albright
dialogue.line: Leslie stole my waffle from the break room refrigerator. Not just any waffle—my homemade Belgian waffle with the pearl sugar that I brought from the UN cafeteria.

jokes.text: Well, I think I've said all I want to say right here. [April's reaction beat to being denied more space]
jokes.setup: April has offered Senator Gillibrand room for a P.S. in the inscription she wrote.
jokes.punchline: The Senator politely but firmly declines to add more — and April presumably reacts with slight disappointment that the Senator won't fully commit to the Leslie worship.
jokes.explanation: A mild topper to the inscription joke. Functional but not as strong as the setup; the Senator's gracious refusal is a reasonable button rather than a great joke.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: I just want to say, April is like Mary J. Blige.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's the nicest thing anyone's ever said to me.

jokes.text: Did anyone ever tell you that your tenacity can be intimidating? [Leslie] Yes. Every month of my life since fourth grade.
jokes.setup: A reluctant senator tells Leslie her persistence is intimidating, as a mild rebuke.
jokes.punchline: Leslie takes it as a compliment and confirms it's been a lifelong pattern since fourth grade — the specificity of 'every month' and 'fourth grade' makes it land.
jokes.explanation: 'Yes. Every month of my life since fourth grade' is a great line — the 'every month' is weirdly specific (not every day, not every year, but every month) and 'fourth grade' grounds it in a real child Leslie. Leslie not only accepts the criticism but has been keeping a mental tally. Strong Leslie character joke.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: I use Comic Sans because it conveys a sense of whimsy, which makes people want to hire me. I also put my references in white text on a white background so they're a surprise when they highlight the page. And I always list my skills in alphabetical order by how much I think about them during the day.

jokes.text: Our real passion is... Polynesian folk music. [Senator] What? [Senator Booker] Our band is playing in Georgetown tonight if you'd like to come. We're called 'Across the Isle.'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Senator Booker are telling a third senator what they have in common beyond parks policy, building to what sounds like a meaningful political passion.
jokes.punchline: The reveal is Polynesian folk music — a totally unexpected hobby — with the bonus that their band is called 'Across the Isle,' a pun.
jokes.explanation: The absurdity of two U.S. senators sharing a Polynesian folk music band is funny on its own. The band name 'Across the Isle' (isle/aisle pun) is good comedy wordplay. The setup of building toward something politically meaningful before landing on ukulele jams is well-structured misdirection.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: April, I'm gonna help you get this job. I'm gonna make the most patriotic display this town has ever seen.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Please don't.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Too late. I've already ordered a life-size cardboard cutout of Bald Eagle riding a motorcycle through the American flag while holding the Constitution and a apple pie.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Why would that help me get a job?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Because America, April. America.

jokes.text: Did you get that? 'Isle'? 'Isle' like an island and then 'across the aisle'? The political 'aisle'? It's, like, a pun. It's a play on words. [third senator] I do get it.
jokes.setup: The band name 'Across the Isle' has just been revealed.
jokes.punchline: Leslie and/or Booker over-explain the pun to the third senator, who drily confirms they understood it — the over-explanation becoming its own joke about political types assuming no one gets nuance.
jokes.explanation: The running explanation of the pun — breaking it down into its components with growing desperation — is a nice comic beat. The senator's flat 'I do get it' is the perfect straight-man response. Leslie's enthusiasm for her own pun is characterful.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I missed the tour of the world's largest ball of twine.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That was last week! Why didn't you tell me?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Because I didn't want to go. I was being sarcastic.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: April, that's in Minnesota. It's a real thing.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I know it's real. That's what makes it worse.

jokes.text: It's $8 if you buy your tickets now. It's $10 at the door. [third senator] A fiscal conservative. Love this guy.
jokes.setup: Senator Booker invites the senator to his Polynesian folk band's show.
jokes.punchline: The third senator's 'A fiscal conservative. Love this guy.' frames the band's modest pricing as a political virtue — a political-world way of interpreting everything through an ideological lens.
jokes.explanation: Funny political satire — the senator can't help but categorize even concert ticket pricing in political terms. 'Love this guy' is a nice sincere button. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You can't look at me during serious conversations. It makes me uncomfortable.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, I won't look at you.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Also, you have to wear shoe-mittens.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What are shoe-mittens?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Mittens for your shoes. It's non-negotiable.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: April, I'm not wearing shoe-mittens.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Fine. Forget the shoe-mittens.

jokes.text: She designed her own major, Halloween Studies.
jokes.setup: Andy and Ben are pitching April to Barney for a consulting position; Barney asks what she majored in.
jokes.punchline: April's college major was 'Halloween Studies' — a made-up, April-specific major that is simultaneously absurd and completely plausible for her.
jokes.explanation: Two words — 'Halloween Studies' — and the joke is complete. Perfectly efficient, deeply character-specific (it could only be April's major), and funny on its own merits as an invented academic discipline. Andy's delivery as if this is obviously fine is key. Highly quotable, rewatch-rewarding. One of the episode's standout moments.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I meant every word of that. You all mean so much to me, and I'm grateful for—

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Anyway, I hope you all die in a fire.

jokes.text: Does that compound your interest? Huh? What do you say? Huh, Barney? [Ben] Ben, that was amazing.
jokes.setup: Ben has been making a pitch to Barney the accountant; Andy interrupts with an accounting pun.
jokes.punchline: 'Does that compound your interest?' is an accounting pun (compound interest) deployed as a persuasion tool, with Andy's insistent 'Huh? Huh, Barney?' revealing his proud confidence in it. Ben's sarcastic 'Ben, that was amazing' is directed at himself — or perhaps Ben made the pun and Andy is praising him.
jokes.explanation: A fun accounting pun that works because of the enthusiasm behind it. 'Huh? Huh, Barney?' adds charm. The callback to Ben's earlier pun enthusiasm creates symmetry. Not as sharp as 'actuarily' but pleasant.

dialogue.speaker: Alyssa
dialogue.line: Remember that gift you gave me last year?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my god, yes! Did you love it?

dialogue.speaker: Alyssa
dialogue.line: It was a pillow with my face on it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A pillow with your beautiful face on it! So you could always have me with you when you sleep.

jokes.text: Holy crap. This is the job for her, I can feel it. She'll take it. Now, let's talk perks. Does she get the summer off? Is it like school?
jokes.setup: Andy and Ben are pitching April to Barney; Barney describes the consulting role.
jokes.punchline: Andy, upon hearing it's a good fit, immediately starts negotiating on April's behalf — but his first perk question is whether she gets summer off like in school, revealing his childlike understanding of employment.
jokes.explanation: 'Is it like school?' is the key phrase — Andy genuinely doesn't know how adult employment differs from school schedules. His confident negotiating posture combined with this ignorance is very funny. The line 'I can feel it' before the absurd perk question is a nice setup.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Alyssa, this is April Ludgate. She's my assistant, and she's absolutely amazing. Brilliant, talented, beautiful...

dialogue.speaker: Alyssa
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, do I know you?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, but I'm just saying April is—

dialogue.speaker: Alyssa
dialogue.line: I think you need to leave me alone.

dialogue.speaker: Alyssa
dialogue.line: Stop following me around, okay? It's weird.

jokes.text: Ben, that was amazing. / Thank you.
jokes.setup: Ben just delivered an accounting pun during a job pitch.
jokes.punchline: Andy's genuine, sincere admiration for Ben's pun — treating it as if it were a brilliant rhetorical move — is funny both because Andy doesn't understand puns and because it's an unexpectedly warm reaction.
jokes.explanation: A functional warm beat between Andy and Ben. Andy's sincere enthusiasm for things he doesn't fully understand is a reliable character note, though this instance is fairly mild.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: It's the perfect job for me. I get to work alone, mostly in the dark, organizing things that are already dead.

jokes.text: Old Norbs is stepping down. Couldn't handle the pressure, huh? What a wuss. [Randy] His marriage is falling apart. [Leslie] Oh! Oh, okay. [Randy] She had an affair with his best friend. [Leslie] Okay. I feel bad about what I said before.
jokes.setup: Randy tells Leslie that Mike Norbert is retiring. Leslie immediately assumes weakness.
jokes.punchline: The escalating revelation — falling apart marriage, infidelity — makes Leslie's casual dismissal ('what a wuss') increasingly uncomfortable, and her belated remorse ('I feel bad about what I said before') is a beat behind the revelations.
jokes.explanation: Well-structured cringe comedy — Leslie's foot-in-mouth moment is escalated by increasingly serious revelations. The structure of 'Oh! Oh, okay.' responding to each new detail is excellent. 'I feel bad about what I said before' being triggered by the affair (not the falling-apart marriage) is a nice grace note.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Everyone's been so nice to me lately. I think I need to bathe in pig's blood to get rid of it.

jokes.text: I have to enroll in SESCDP? Forty-four weeks of intensive courses and note-taking? Um, it's a dream come true.
jokes.setup: Randy tells Leslie she'd have to complete the Senior Executive Service Candidate Development Program.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's pause before 'Um, it's a dream come true' signals that she briefly processes this as a burden before her enthusiasm kicks in and she reframes forty-four weeks of intensive government courses as a dream.
jokes.explanation: The 'Um' before 'it's a dream come true' is the whole joke — Leslie processing something most people would find crushing as exciting is perfect Leslie. Her reciting the exact program name and duration suggests she already knows what it entails, making the reversal funnier.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Everyone's being so nice to me. It's weird. I don't know what to do with myself. I guess I'll just go home and practice my stabbing.

jokes.text: A freaking confirmation hearing? Excuse me a second. What's that? Mmm-hmm. Mmm-hmm. To the best of my recollection, yes, I accept the job.
jokes.setup: Randy warns Leslie there will be a confirmation hearing for the Deputy Director position.
jokes.punchline: Leslie stages a fake phone call, then treats her own internal deliberation as a congressional hearing, giving testimony to herself ('to the best of my recollection') before accepting.
jokes.explanation: 'To the best of my recollection' is the key phrase — Leslie immediately adopts formal confirmation hearing language for a completely internal conversation. The fake phone call bit is a classic farce device, but the specific choice of confirmation hearing testimony language makes it fresh. Strong character integration: Leslie's entire identity is government, so of course she frames her own decision-making in government procedural terms.

jokes.text: Excuse me, ma'am. Do you mind if I borrow your hat? I just want to throw it up in the air victoriously. [stranger] No. [Leslie] Ma'am?
jokes.setup: Leslie has just accepted a career-defining promotion and is overwhelmed with joy.
jokes.punchline: Rather than celebrating normally, Leslie tries to borrow a stranger's hat specifically to recreate the iconic Mary Tyler Moore hat-toss — and is denied.
jokes.explanation: A Mary Tyler Moore reference that works even without knowledge of it — the image of Leslie asking a stranger to borrow their hat to throw victoriously is funny on its own. 'I just want to throw it up in the air victoriously' is a great line. The persistence of 'Ma'am?' after being rejected adds to it. Strong Leslie character work.

jokes.text: Simple solution? I break into her college and I change her degree to accounting. Easy. On my way out, look up at the blackboard. What is that? Impossible math equation? I solve it. X equals Y, obviously. Professor comes up to me, he says, 'I've been working on that for 50 years. Why don't you accept this math trophy?' By the time he turns around, I'm gone.
jokes.setup: The group is brainstorming how to make April seem qualified for the consulting job; Andy is asked for ideas in a talking-head.
jokes.punchline: Andy's 'simple solution' escalates from 'break into a college and change a degree' to solving an impossible math equation while leaving, to receiving a math trophy, to mysteriously vanishing — an increasingly elaborate fantasy delivered with total confidence.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a genuine standout Parks and Rec moment. The structure is near-perfect: starts as a simple (if illegal) plan, then escalates into a full action-movie fantasy with 'X equals Y, obviously' being the peak absurdist detail (Andy confidently solving a famous unsolvable equation with total wrongness). 'By the time he turns around, I'm gone' is a cinematic exit that completes the fantasy. The escalation is disciplined — each beat tops the last. Strong argument for approaching the 8.0+ calibration threshold.

jokes.text: It's just a signed photograph of a puppet named ALF.
jokes.setup: Ben is showing the team April's original Parks Department job application, suggesting they update her résumé.
jokes.punchline: April's original application was a signed photo of ALF — the 1980s alien puppet — rather than an actual résumé.
jokes.explanation: Instant classic absurdist joke. The specificity of ALF (not just 'a puppet' or 'a TV character') is the key — it's exactly the right level of obscure-but-recognizable. That this is April's actual résumé tells you everything about her character. Ben's deadpan delivery is implied and perfect. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Fountains. Water. Sky. You. Looking at me like a crazy person.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks April to look around and say what she sees, trying to inspire April about their possible future in D.C.
jokes.punchline: April lists banal things with no enthusiasm, culminating in including Leslie's concerned expression in her inventory of the scene.
jokes.explanation: The construction of the list followed by 'You. Looking at me like a crazy person' is excellent. April subverts the inspirational question by being maximally literal and then roasting Leslie's expression in the same flat tone. Great economy and character-specific.

jokes.text: Wow, Leslie. I haven't seen you this upset since you almost forgot Ann's half-birthday.
jokes.setup: Leslie is venting about April's decision to quit to her lunch companion (revealed to be Madeleine Albright).
jokes.punchline: Madeleine Albright casually references Leslie's half-birthday tracking of Ann as the benchmark for Leslie's emotional states — the absurdity being that a former Secretary of State knows this about Leslie.
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Leslie's lunch companion is Madeleine Albright is a wonderful Parks-style celebrity cameo payoff. 'Ann's half-birthday' is already a great Leslie-specific detail (of course Leslie tracks half-birthdays), and the idea that Albright knows and references this fact is both absurd and delightful. Strong rewatch bonus.

jokes.text: Leslie's talking head: 'I love her, but you spend so much time and effort on someone's life and she's just going to quit on me? It's like, what's the point?'
jokes.setup: April has just quit; Leslie is processing it.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's framing of April's career decision as something done specifically 'to her' — 'quit on me' — is both funny and deeply Leslie. Her existential crisis ('what's the point?') over losing a mentee is comedically self-centered.
jokes.explanation: A gentle character comedy beat — Leslie's instinct to make everything about herself is both funny and the episode's emotional conflict. Not a huge laugh but a good character observation.

jokes.text: Well, because when I knew I would be coming to Washington to work, I wore you down until you agreed to become my friend.
jokes.setup: Madeleine Albright is pointing out how many lunches they've had.
jokes.punchline: Leslie explains that she simply wore down a former Secretary of State through sheer persistence until she agreed to be her friend — treating international diplomacy and personal friendship-making as the same negotiation.
jokes.explanation: The idea of Leslie 'wearing down' Madeleine Albright into friendship applies her standard persistence technique to an extraordinary target. It's also a callback to the senator's earlier remark about Leslie's intimidating tenacity — suggesting she uses this approach on everyone.

jokes.text: But sometimes, you're so focused and driven that you forget about people's feelings. / Name one time I've done that. / Well, you were so wrapped up in your story that you actually ate my waffle.
jokes.setup: Madeleine Albright gently criticizes Leslie for being too focused and forgetting people's feelings. Leslie challenges her to name a time.
jokes.punchline: The example Madeleine Albright reaches for — Leslie absent-mindedly eating Albright's waffle — is both absurdly small and clearly genuine, which makes it very funny.
jokes.explanation: The contrast between Madeleine Albright (former Secretary of State) and a waffle theft is excellent comedy. The joke is that Albright has plenty of serious examples she could cite but lands on the most relatable, mundane grievance — and it still illustrates the point. Leslie eating someone's waffle while talking is perfectly Leslie.

jokes.text: Well, you were so wrapped up in your story that you actually ate my waffle.
jokes.setup: Madeleine Albright is giving Leslie an example of times she's been so focused she forgets about people's feelings.
jokes.punchline: The example is that Leslie ate Albright's waffle while wrapped up in her own story — a petty, very human complaint delivered by a former Secretary of State.
jokes.explanation: The bathos of Madeleine Albright's grievance being 'she ate my waffle' is excellent. The waffle is so mundane — it's not a policy disagreement or a diplomatic incident, it's a breakfast item. Leslie's absentminded waffle consumption as her great character flaw is also very her.

jokes.text: You're right, once again, Madeleine Albright.
jokes.setup: Albright has just dispensed wisdom about letting people make their own choices.
jokes.punchline: Leslie addresses her by full name — 'Madeleine Albright' — as if to ensure the audience/herself understands the weight of this person's advice, which makes the casualness of the friendship funnier.
jokes.explanation: Using someone's full formal name in casual conversation is a Leslie-specific tick and signals both awe and comfort. Functional joke, solid character beat.

jokes.text: Can I have my pin back now? [Leslie] Oh! Oh, yeah, sorry. Thank you for letting me wear it. It just makes me feel very powerful. [Albright] Me, too.
jokes.setup: Leslie and Albright have been having lunch; Albright asks for her pin back.
jokes.punchline: Leslie has been wearing Madeleine Albright's signature brooch/pin during lunch, and both women agree it makes them feel powerful — the visual of Leslie wearing the Albright pin while arguing about National Parks is inherently funny.
jokes.explanation: Madeleine Albright's famous brooches are a real cultural touchstone, making this a layered joke — Leslie borrowed the actual Albright diplomatic pin. 'It just makes me feel very powerful. [Albright] Me, too.' is a perfect two-line button: Albright confirming that yes, the pin works on her as well. Rewatch bonus for catching the visual of Leslie in the pin throughout their scene.

jokes.text: And $500 cash, in case you want to go the straight-up bribe route. [Ben] Donna.
jokes.setup: The team is assembling April's presentation for Barney; Donna describes her contribution.
jokes.punchline: Donna casually includes $500 cash as a contingency bribery fund, treating it as a standard professional resource.
jokes.explanation: Donna's pragmatic, no-nonsense willingness to bribe is a character-consistent gag. 'In case you want to go the straight-up bribe route' frames it as merely one strategy among many, which is the best part. Ben's single-word response 'Donna' does appropriate work.

jokes.text: You put me on the team, I find a way to win.
jokes.setup: Ben has just said 'Donna' in mild rebuke after the bribe offer.
jokes.punchline: Donna responds with pure, confident self-regard — treating the bribe as the sign of a winner's mentality.
jokes.explanation: A nice Donna character moment — she frames bribery as competitive strategy, not corruption. The confidence is funny. Shorter and less original than the bribe reveal but a decent button.

jokes.text: I went through quite a few staples.
jokes.setup: Garry is describing his contribution to the April presentation — copying, collating, and stapling.
jokes.punchline: His contribution note at the end is that he used a lot of staples — the comedy being that this is both his entire contribution and that he feels it's worth mentioning.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Garry joke — his contribution is entirely clerical, and his mention of staple consumption as a notable fact is deeply Garry. The understatement is the humor: this is all he has to offer, and he's slightly proud of it.

jokes.text: I added a personal testimony vouching for April's brilliance. And this guy better appreciate it, because I do not compare people to Mary J. Blige lightly.
jokes.setup: Donna is describing her contribution to the presentation package.
jokes.punchline: Donna has compared April to Mary J. Blige in a professional recommendation letter, and treats this as a serious honor.
jokes.explanation: 'I do not compare people to Mary J. Blige lightly' is an excellent Donna line — the specificity of MJB as the ultimate benchmark for excellence is both absurd and completely in character for Donna. Ben's response 'Uh, no one should' is a perfectly dry validation. One of the better lines in the episode.

jokes.text: Do you want to go to dinner tonight? [Craig] I do not. [Donna] Respect. [Craig] I'm free. [Donna] I have plans.
jokes.setup: After the team meeting wraps, Craig asks Donna to dinner.
jokes.punchline: Craig immediately rejects his own suggestion ('I do not'), then reverses to say he's free; Donna, validated by the rejection, now claims she has plans. The rapid reversal creates a comedic chase-reject pattern.
jokes.explanation: A four-line exchange that's remarkably efficient. Craig's 'I do not' → 'I'm free' reversal and Donna's mirror-opposite reversal is sharp, fast comedy. 'Respect' as Donna's response to the rejection is a great character beat. The entire joke takes 5 seconds.

jokes.text: Give me the job! My name's April Ludgate, and my talent is explosive. Go USA! USA! USA!
jokes.setup: Ben says he has a plan to go the 'extra mile' for April's application.
jokes.punchline: Andy's video audition tape (implied by context) consists of him shouting April's name, claiming her talent is 'explosive,' and launching into USA chants — a completely unhinged piece of advocacy.
jokes.explanation: 'My talent is explosive' combined with the USA chants is a wonderfully unhinged advocacy video. Andy's patriotic pivot makes absolutely no sense in context, which is perfect. 'Give me the job!' as his opening for someone else's application is great Andy logic.

jokes.text: Yeah, well, I had to miss the 'Memorable Rain Gutters of Washington' walking tour, so this better be good.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks April to come meet her somewhere; April shows up.
jokes.punchline: April sarcastically references a walking tour she had to skip ('Memorable Rain Gutters of Washington') that is clearly a parody of Leslie's Historical Lampposts tour — even more mundane.
jokes.explanation: A perfect callback and escalation — April's parody version of Leslie's lamppost tour is even more specific and boring (rain gutters vs. lampposts). It's a callback that rewards attentive viewers and demonstrates April has been listening to Leslie's suggestions with sardonic intent. 'This better be good' lands well. One of the better April lines in the episode.

jokes.text: Now take your shoes off and wear them like mittens. [Leslie] April. [April] Okay, sorry.
jokes.setup: April asks Leslie to turn around because she's about to say something serious and can't do it facing her — then asks Leslie to take her shoes off and wear them like mittens.
jokes.punchline: April, committed to her own self-protection from emotional vulnerability, adds a shoe-mitten demand as an emotional distance strategy — then immediately retreats when challenged.
jokes.explanation: 'Wear them like mittens' is a wonderfully specific absurdist demand that reveals how hard April works to deflect sincerity. The immediate 'Okay, sorry' retreat is honest and endearing. 'April. / Okay, sorry.' is a two-beat exchange that feels very real. Good economy and strong character integration.

jokes.text: And I love you very much. Which is why I have decided not to turn you into a sea urchin. Which I could do because I am an actual witch with powers and I'm evil...
jokes.setup: April has just delivered a genuine, heartfelt speech of gratitude to Leslie — the most sincere she's ever been.
jokes.punchline: April can't let the sincerity stand and immediately pivots to claiming she's a witch who chose not to turn Leslie into a sea urchin, framing the sparing as the actual gift.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode and a standout April moment. The structural genius is that April gives a genuinely moving speech and then immediately, inevitably, has to undo it — but the way she undoes it (sea urchin, actual witch, evil) is perfectly April. 'Which I could do because I am an actual witch with powers' said with apparent sincerity is the core of her character: dark, absurdist, self-protecting through supernatural claims. The specificity of 'sea urchin' (not a toad or a rat — a sea urchin) is inspired. The comedic moment is earned by the emotional setup.

jokes.text: [Leslie] I know. [April] And I hate everything. [Leslie] I know you do. I know.
jokes.setup: April is insisting on her evil witch identity to deflect from her sincere speech.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's 'I know' to all of April's claims — the evil, the powers, the hatred — is delivered with complete warm acceptance. Leslie accepting April's witch persona is an affectionate joke about how well she knows her.
jokes.explanation: The repeated 'I know' from Leslie — calm, warm, utterly unfazed — is a character comedy masterclass. Leslie's acceptance of April's evil as a simple fact of their friendship, combined with the previous emotional beat, makes this both funny and genuinely touching. The 'I know you do. I know.' cadence is perfect.

jokes.text: I found this crazy woman on the street and she won't leave me alone.
jokes.setup: Leslie introduces April to Alyssa at the American Service Foundation, calling her 'the single greatest human being ever.'
jokes.punchline: April immediately undercuts Leslie's effusive introduction by claiming she just found Leslie on the street, inverting the power dynamic and suggesting Leslie is the burden.
jokes.explanation: A nice reversal — Leslie treating April as her precious mentee vs. April treating Leslie as an annoying stray. The timing directly after Leslie's 'single greatest human being' speech makes it land well.

jokes.text: Two days later, we had set up the entire program, and she sent me a throw pillow with my face stitched onto it. [Leslie] Not my best work. Plus, you changed your hair. I'm going to send you another one.
jokes.setup: Alyssa is describing her previous experience with Leslie's enthusiasm.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's two-part response — first self-critiquing the pillow quality, then promising another one because Alyssa changed her hair — escalates from odd to genuinely unsettling in the best Leslie way.
jokes.explanation: The face-pillow is already an unnerving gift, but Leslie's response — 'not my best work' and the immediate commitment to an updated pillow because of a haircut — is the joke. It's Leslie's gift-giving taken to a slightly invasive extreme, framed with total sincerity. 'Plus, you changed your hair' as the reason for a second pillow is exactly right.

jokes.text: I don't know, Madeleine. They're taking forever, and I'm starting to lose it. Talk to me, okay? Your voice makes me calm. Tell me another Yeltsin story.
jokes.setup: Leslie is waiting outside while April meets with Alyssa, getting anxious.
jokes.punchline: Leslie is apparently on the phone with Madeleine Albright again, asking her to tell another Yeltsin story as a calming technique — the absurdity of Albright's Yeltsin anecdotes as Leslie's anxiety remedy.
jokes.explanation: A callback to the Albright friendship that deepens it beautifully. 'Tell me another Yeltsin story' is the perfect punch — Albright's diplomatic history with Yeltsin as Leslie's version of a lullaby. The specificity of Yeltsin (not 'a foreign leader story' but Yeltsin specifically) is exactly right. This is one of the episode's most quotable lines.

jokes.text: Okay, she's here. I have to go. Bye. Say hi to your daughters.
jokes.setup: Leslie has been using Madeleine Albright as a phone anxiety remedy while waiting.
jokes.punchline: Leslie dismisses Albright with a casual 'say hi to your daughters' — treating the former Secretary of State like a neighbor who lives down the street.
jokes.explanation: The casualness of ending the call with a 'say hi to your daughters' — a normal neighborly sign-off applied to Madeleine Albright — is the joke. It completes the bit of treating this extraordinary person as a close friend perfectly.

jokes.text: I want to tell people what to do, and then send them far away from me.
jokes.setup: April comes out of her meeting and explains what she wants to do — work at the American Service Foundation matching people with jobs.
jokes.punchline: April's job description is 'tell people what to do and send them far away from me' — reframing career counseling as a system for maximizing her own isolation.
jokes.explanation: Excellent April line. 'Tell people what to do, and then send them far away from me' reframes a helping profession as a misanthropic power fantasy — and makes it sound ideal. The economy is near-perfect: nine words that tell you exactly who April is. One of the most quotable lines in the episode, and it's also genuinely touching because it IS actually a perfect job for her. Character integration is exceptional.

jokes.text: I feel like I need to take a shower in pig's blood to wash all the niceness off me.
jokes.setup: April is touched by how much everyone has been helping her find a new job.
jokes.punchline: April reacts to kindness with a Carrie-esque image of pig's blood as the antidote to niceness — framing generosity as a contaminant she needs to purge.
jokes.explanation: One of the best April lines in the episode. The horror movie imagery (pig's blood shower = Carrie) used as a hygiene metaphor for removing emotional warmth is perfectly April. 'Wash all the niceness off me' as the stated goal is both funny and character-revealing — she experiences kindness as a physical substance requiring removal. Highly quotable, deeply character-specific.

jokes.text: So, long story short, we might have found you the perfect job. But also, I might have blown it. Ben and Ron are there now to try to fix it. And if they don't, I feel like it's kind of on them.
jokes.setup: Andy updates April on the consulting job situation.
jokes.punchline: Andy cheerfully summarizes that he might have ruined everything and then casually assigns the blame to Ben and Ron — completely unconcerned about the chaos he caused.
jokes.explanation: 'If they don't, I feel like it's kind of on them' is Andy's specific form of accountability — he won't acknowledge fault, but he also doesn't seem upset, which makes it funnier. Good character voice.

jokes.text: Ben and Ron's pitch to Barney for April, ending with Ron: 'Please don't hold anything Andy did against April.'
jokes.setup: Ben and Ron are making a final push to get Barney to consider April for the consulting job.
jokes.punchline: Ron's contribution to the pitch is explicitly asking Barney to ignore everything Andy did — implying Andy's involvement was so destructive it needs specific disavowal.
jokes.explanation: A good implicit joke about Andy's reliability as a helper. Ron's specific need to preemptively apologize for Andy's behavior says everything without saying it.

jokes.text: You know what? If her friends are trying this hard, there must be something amazing about her.
jokes.setup: Ron and Ben have just finished a passionate pitch for April to Barney, who was skeptical.
jokes.punchline: Barney's logic — that the effort of the friends proves April's worth rather than April's own credentials — is both touching and slightly absurd as a hiring criterion.
jokes.explanation: Functional setup for the upcoming reversal (April already has another job). The joke is mild — the logic is sweet but the comedy is mostly in service of plot. Weakest section of the episode approaching the denouement.

jokes.text: Oh, boy. Okay. She doesn't want the job.
jokes.setup: Ron and Ben have secured April an interview with Barney. They call April to tell her the good news.
jokes.punchline: April, having already found her real career path moments earlier, immediately deflates all their hard work with 'She doesn't want the job.'
jokes.explanation: 'Oh, boy. Okay.' followed by 'She doesn't want the job' — delivered as a complete, undramatic announcement — is a great closing joke. The brevity and matter-of-factness is perfectly April. The pivot from good news to dismissal is tight.

jokes.text: I see. [long beat] Well, this is uncomfortable.
jokes.setup: Barney has just been told that April, on whose behalf he's been extensively courted, doesn't want the job he just agreed to offer her.
jokes.punchline: After a beat of silence, Barney's 'Well, this is uncomfortable' is a masterpiece of understatement — the comedy is in the pause, the acknowledgment, and the complete lack of drama in his delivery.
jokes.explanation: The episode's closing joke and it's a perfect button. The pause before 'Well, this is uncomfortable' is the actual joke — the silence contains the comedy. The line itself is funny in its total calm understatement of what is genuinely awkward. 'I see.' as the initial response is also good. A strong ending that doesn't oversell itself.

tmdb_overview: While Leslie and April take a business trip to Washington, April wrestles with her future. Back in Pawnee, Andy tries to find April the perfect job.
insight: Escalation-driven finale trades peak density for character-grounded absurdism.
